title: Strongly transcendental element over a reduced subring kills quasi-finiteness
statement: Let $R\subseteq S$ be a subring of a commutative ring, with $R$ and $S$ reduced (no nonzero nilpotent elements). Let $x\in S$ be strongly transcendental over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-strongly-transcendental] (for the inclusion $R\to S$), and assume that $S$ is a finitely generated module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] over the subring $R[x]\subseteq S$ generated by $R$ and $x$ (so $R\to S$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]). Then $R\to S$ is not quasi-finite at any prime ideal of $S$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime].

proof.text:
*A minimal prime below $\mathfrak q$.* Let $\mathfrak q\subset S$ be any prime ideal. By [lem-weil-pbc-prime-contains-minimal-prime] (with $I=0$) there is a minimal prime ideal $\mathfrak q'\subseteq\mathfrak q$ of $S$. Put $\mathfrak p'=R\cap\mathfrak q'$, $ ar R=R/\mathfrak p'$, $ ar S=S/\mathfrak q'$. The kernel of $R	o S	o ar S$ is $R\cap\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak p'$, so the induced map $ ar R	o ar S$ is injective and we regard $ ar R$ as a subring of $ ar S$. $ ar S$ is an integral domain since $\mathfrak q'$ is prime, hence so is its subring $ ar R$ ($ ar R

proof.text: *Strong transcendence modulo $\mathfrak q'$.* Since $R\subseteq S$ are reduced, $x$ is strongly transcendental over $R$ and $\mathfrak q'$ is a minimal prime of $S$ with $\mathfrak p'=R\cap\mathfrak q'$, [lem-weil-pbc-strongly-transcendental-quotient-minimal-prime] says that the image $\bar x$ of $x$ in $\bar S$ is strongly transcendental over $\bar R$ [def-weil-pbc-strongly-transcendental] for the inclusion $\bar R\subseteq\bar S$ of step 1.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00Q2 (lemma-reduced-strongly-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30714)

proof.text: *Finiteness modulo $\mathfrak q'$, and finite type.* Let $s_1,\dots,s_m\in S$ generate $S$ as an $R[x]$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], so every $s\in S$ is $\sum_jc_js_j$ with $c_j\in R[x]$, i.e. $c_j$ a polynomial expression in $x$ with coefficients in $R$. Reducing modulo $\mathfrak q'$, the image of $c_j$ is the same polynomial expression in $\bar x$ with coefficients in $\bar R$, so it lies in the subring $\bar R[\bar x]\subseteq\bar S$, and since $S\to\bar S$ is surjective, $\bar s_1,\dots,\bar s_m$ generate $\bar S$ as an $\bar R[\bar x]$-module. Likewise $S$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by $x,s_1,\dots,s_m$, so $R\to S$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] (and so is $\bar R\to\bar S$, generated by $\bar x,\bar s_1,\dots,\bar s_m$).

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00Q2 (lemma-reduced-strongly-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30714)

proof.text: *The domain case.* By steps 1-3, $\bar R\subseteq\bar S$ are integral domains, $\bar x\in\bar S$ is strongly transcendental over $\bar R$ and $\bar S$ is a finitely generated $\bar R[\bar x]$-module. By [lem-weil-pbc-domains-strongly-transcendental-not-quasi-finite], $\bar R\to\bar S$ is not quasi-finite [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime] at any prime of $\bar S$; in particular not at $\bar{\mathfrak q}=\mathfrak q/\mathfrak q'$, which is a prime ideal of $\bar S$ (as $\mathfrak q'\subseteq\mathfrak q$) whose inverse image in $S$ is $\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00Q2 (lemma-reduced-strongly-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30714)

proof.text: *Back to $R\to S$ by the four rings lemma.* The square formed by $R\to S$, $R\to\bar R$, $\bar R\to\bar S$ and $S\to\bar S$ commutes (both composites $R\to\bar S$ are $a\mapsto a\bmod\mathfrak q'$). $R\to S$ is of finite type (step 3), and every element of $\bar S$ is the image of an element of $S$ (a sum $\sigma\cdot1$ with $\sigma$ in the image of $S$ and $1$ in the image of $\bar R$), so $S\otimes_R\bar R\to\bar S$ is surjective. The prime $\bar{\mathfrak q}\subset\bar S$ has inverse image $\mathfrak q$ in $S$ (step 4). Suppose $R\to S$ were quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. Then [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-four-rings] (with $R'=\bar R$, $S'=\bar S$, $\mathfrak q'=\bar{\mathfrak q}$) gives that $\bar R\to\bar S$ is quasi-finite at $\bar{\mathfrak q}$, contradicting step 4. Hence $R\to S$ is not quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$; as $\mathfrak q$ was an arbitrary prime of $S$, the lemma follows.
